title: The Homogeneous MeerKAT and Swift/XRT X-ray Binary Radio:X-ray Plane
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. The website accompanying this paper, including the full data release, can be found at: https://thunderkat.physics.ox.ac.uk/
summary: During the hard and quiescent spectral states in X-ray binaries, a non-linear correlation is observed between radio and X-ray luminosities, providing a valuable tool to probe the connection between accretion and jet production. This relation was originally thought to define a single 'standard' correlation spanning several orders of magnitude in X-ray luminosity, and was extended to active galactic nuclei by including a mass term. However, subsequent studies revealed a more complex picture, with some sources deviating from the standard correlation and instead populating distinct tracks. To date, all large studies of the radio:X-ray plane have combined data from multiple telescopes, introducing uncertainties due to differing instrument systematics and flux conversions between observing frequencies, thereby complicating comparisons and limiting constraints. ThunderKAT was a five-year programme on the MeerKAT radio telescope that monitored X-ray binaries in outburst, and ran alongside SwiftKAT which provided quasi-simultaneous Swift/XRT X-ray coverage. We present the full set of light curves from these programmes, comprising 948 radio and 1029 X-ray data points. An important finding is the frequent detection of unresolved radio emission during the soft state, likely dominated by previously launched jet ejecta. Using these data, we construct the largest, observationally homogeneous X-ray binary radio:X-ray plane to date. We relate these results to the physical mechanisms proposed to drive inter-source diversity, and outline directions for future observational and theoretical work. This paper is accompanied by a public data release of the ThunderKAT and SwiftKAT measurements and a compiled radio:X-ray plane, available through an interactive website.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the largest observationally homogeneous radio:X-ray plane for X-ray binaries using ThunderKAT (MeerKAT) and SwiftKAT (Swift/XRT) data, comprising 948 radio and 1029 X-ray data points, revealing frequent unresolved radio emission in the soft state and complex deviations from the standard radio-X-ray correlation.
AI.motivation: To construct a large, observationally homogeneous radio:X-ray plane for X-ray binaries, overcoming uncertainties from combining multi-telescope data, in order to better understand the accretion-jet connection and inter-source diversity in the radio-X-ray correlation.
AI.method: ThunderKAT (MeerKAT radio telescope) monitored X-ray binaries over five years, with quasi-simultaneous Swift/XRT X-ray coverage from SwiftKAT; 948 radio and 1029 X-ray data points were compiled into a homogeneous dataset.
AI.result: Frequent detection of unresolved radio emission during the soft state, likely from previously launched jet ejecta; construction of the largest observationally homogeneous radio:X-ray plane for X-ray binaries to date.
AI.conclusion: The homogeneous dataset provides improved constraints on the radio-X-ray correlation and its diversity, relates results to physical mechanisms driving inter-source variation, and outlines future directions; data are publicly released via an interactive website.

title: Reconstructing the Stripping History of the Sagittarius Stream with Neural Networks
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, accepted for Publication in ApJ
summary: The Sagittarius (Sgr) Stream is produced by the ongoing disruption of the Sgr dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxy and is thought to contain multiple wraps that were stripped during different pericentric passages. In this study, we introduce a neural-network--based method trained on $N$-body simulations to infer the stripping time of Sgr Stream stars directly from their phase-space coordinates. We combine spectroscopic data from SEGUE, APOGEE DR17, and LAMOST DR7 LRS with \textit{Gaia} EDR3 astrometry and distance estimates from the latest \texttt{StarHorse} catalog to identify high-quality Sgr Stream members. Applying our method to these stars, we measure a clear metallicity gradient with stripping time, well described by a linear relation with slope $\sim 0.3~\mathrm{dex~Gyr^{-1}}$. We further predict the stripping times of globular clusters previously suggested to originate from the Sgr dSph. M 54, Terzan 7, Terzan 8, and Arp 2 exhibit stripping times consistent with being currently bound to the Sgr remnant. Pal 12, Whiting 1, and NGC 2419 are inferred to have been stripped $0.9 \pm 0.1$, $1.1 \pm 0.2$, and $2.1 \pm 0.2$ Gyr ago, respectively. For NGC 4147 and NGC 5634, whose membership in the Sgr system remains uncertain, our analysis suggests stripping times of $1.1 \pm 0.4$ and $1.1 \pm 0.1$ Gyr, respectively, if they are ultimately confirmed as genuine Sgr members. These results demonstrate that data-driven models of dynamical stripping histories offer a promising approach for reconstructing the formation and chemical evolution of the Sgr Stream.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a neural-network-based method trained on N-body simulations to infer the stripping times of Sagittarius Stream stars from phase-space coordinates. Using spectroscopic and astrometric data, they measure a metallicity gradient (~0.3 dex/Gyr) along the stream and predict stripping times for associated globular clusters.
AI.motivation: To reconstruct the dynamical stripping history of the Sagittarius Stream and understand its formation and chemical evolution by inferring stripping times of individual stars and globular clusters.
AI.method: A neural-network model trained on N-body simulations was developed to infer stripping times directly from phase-space coordinates. High-quality Sgr Stream members were identified using SEGUE, APOGEE DR17, LAMOST DR7 LRS, Gaia EDR3 astrometry, and StarHorse distance estimates.
AI.result: A clear metallicity gradient with stripping time was found, following a linear relation of slope ~0.3 dex/Gyr. Stripping times were predicted for globular clusters: Pal 12 (0.9±0.1 Gyr), Whiting 1 (1.1±0.2 Gyr), NGC 2419 (2.1±0.2 Gyr), and for uncertain members NGC 4147 (1.1±0.4 Gyr) and NGC 5634 (1.1±0.1 Gyr). M 54, Terzan 7, Terzan 8, and Arp 2 appear currently bound to the Sgr remnant.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven models of dynamical stripping histories are a promising approach for reconstructing the formation and chemical evolution of the Sgr Stream.

title: Planets in Pulsar Winds
summary: Planets around pulsars were the first discovered exoplanets, found thanks to the extremely precise pulsar timing. Here we suggest that they could also be found through the radio emission generated by the pulsar-planet magnetospheric interaction. We present the results of special relativistic numerical simulations of planets in a pulsar wind of velocity $v=0.985~c$, corresponding to a Lorentz factor $γ=5.795$. Planets, modeled as a perfectly conducting solid surface in an external magnetic field originating from the pulsar, produce radio emission in the extended magnetic structure on the planet's nightside. We find that the planet around a known pulsar, PSR J0636+5129 b, could be detected via its radio emission. We outline the observational prospects for such objects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that planets around pulsars, traditionally detected via pulsar timing, could instead be found through radio emissions generated by the interaction between the pulsar wind and the planet's magnetosphere. Using special relativistic simulations, the authors model a planet in a high-velocity pulsar wind (Lorentz factor γ=5.795) and show that the planet produces detectable radio emission on its nightside. They identify PSR J0636+5129 b as a candidate for such detection and discuss observational prospects.
AI.motivation: To explore an alternative method for detecting pulsar planets via radio emissions from the pulsar-planet magnetospheric interaction, beyond the standard pulsar timing technique.
AI.method: Special relativistic numerical simulations of planets modeled as perfectly conducting solid surfaces in a pulsar wind with velocity v=0.985c (Lorentz factor γ=5.795), under an external magnetic field originating from the pulsar.
AI.result: The planet around the known pulsar PSR J0636+5129 b produces radio emission in the extended magnetic structure on its nightside, potentially detectable via its radio signature.
AI.conclusion: Pulsar planets could be detected via radio emission from the pulsar-planet magnetospheric interaction, offering a complementary detection method to pulsar timing.

title: An Updated Characterization of Luminous Lyα emitters at the End of Reionization
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, submitted to ApJL, comments welcome
summary: We present a multi-wavelength physical characterization of 14 luminous Ly$α$ emitters (LAEs) at $z\approx6$, integrating deep ground-based Magellan/M2FS spectroscopy with heterogeneous JWST/NIRCam broad- and medium-band imaging. Identified via strong Ly$α$ lines with extreme Ly$α$ luminosities of ${>}10^{42.6}$ erg s$^{-1}$, the sample exhibits very large rest-frame equivalent widths (${\gtrsim}100$ Å) and steeply blue UV continua ($β_{\rm median}\simeq-2.2$, $-18.2>M_{\rm 1500}>-20.2$ mag). Crucially, the integration of NIRCam medium-band photometry (F410M) breaks the degeneracy between strong rest-optical nebular emission and Balmer breaks, resolving prior mass overestimations. The tightly constrained spectral energy distribution modeling demonstrates that these luminous LAEs tend to be unequivocally low-mass, ultra-young dwarf starbursts; half the sample is characterized by stellar masses of $M_* < 10^8 M_{\odot}$, ages $\lesssim10$ Myr, and negligible dust attenuation. We also map the production efficiency of ionizing photons and Ly$α$ escape fractions ($f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα}$). The $f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα}$ values are exceptionally high, with a median of ${\gtrsim}40$%, increasing for the bluer UV continua. Finally, analyzing spatial offsets between the Ly$α$ centroid and the stellar counterpart, we demonstrate empirically that internal dust content, rather than neutral hydrogen gas, dominate the suppression of Ly$α$ radiative transfer. Our study reveals that strong Ly$α$ emission of the luminous LAEs are generally attributed to both the vigorous starburst activities and the high $f_{\rm esc}^{\rm Lyα}$. Resembling Lyman continuum leakers, these extreme dwarf systems function as highly efficient ionizing engines at the conclusion of the Epoch of Reionization.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes 14 luminous Lyα emitters (LAEs) at z≈6 using Magellan/M2FS spectroscopy and JWST/NIRCam imaging. These are ultra-young, low-mass dwarf starbursts (half with M* < 10^8 M⊙, ages <10 Myr) with extreme Lyα luminosities, high Lyα escape fractions (median >40%), and negligible dust. Medium-band NIRCam photometry resolves prior mass overestimates. The study shows internal dust, not neutral hydrogen, dominates Lyα suppression, and these systems resemble Lyman continuum leakers that efficiently ionized the universe at the end of the Epoch of Reionization.
AI.motivation: To physically characterize luminous Lyα emitters at z≈6, resolve degeneracies between nebular emission and Balmer breaks in SED modeling, and understand what drives their strong Lyα emission (starburst activity vs. escape fraction).
AI.method: Integrated deep ground-based Magellan/M2FS spectroscopy with JWST/NIRCam broad- and medium-band (F410M) imaging for 14 LAEs at z≈6, performing SED fitting with medium-band photometry to break the nebular emission/Balmer break degeneracy, plus spatial offset analysis between Lyα centroid and stellar continuum.
AI.result: LAEs are ultra-young (<10 Myr), low-mass dwarf starbursts (half with M* < 10^8 M⊙), with steep blue UV continua (β_median≈-2.2), negligible dust, very high Lyα escape fractions (median >40%), and internal dust (not neutral H I) dominates Lyα suppression.
AI.conclusion: Strong Lyα emission in luminous LAEs arises from both vigorous starburst activity and high escape fractions. These extreme dwarf systems are efficient ionizing engines resembling Lyman continuum leakers, playing a key role in reionization at z≈6.

title: The compact neutron star in 4U 1746-37 revisited: Reassessing the mass and radius
summary: A recent analysis of photospheric radius expansion X-ray bursts from the low-mass X-ray binary 4U 1746-37 reported unusually small mass and radius estimates for the neutron star, suggesting it could be a quark star or quark-cluster star. Here, we propose an alternative interpretation: the star's mass and radius could be underestimated from significant blocking of the X-ray flux. Significant blocking factors ($\mathcal{B} \gtrsim 0.8$, reducing the observed flux to $\sim17\%$ of the intrinsic emission) permit neutron star parameters consistent with the canonical values: $M = 1.59 \pm 0.69 M_{\odot}$, $R = 13.0 \pm 5.45\,\mathrm{km}$, or $M = 2.12 \pm 1.08 M_{\odot}$, $R = 9.80 \pm 4.13\,\mathrm{km}$. The blocking factor, which varies with the photospheric radius, provides a natural explanation for the anomalously large peak-to-touchdown flux ratio ($\sim2.0$) and highlights the importance of accounting for geometric system configuration in neutron star mass--radius estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that unexpectedly small mass/radius estimates for 4U 1746-37's neutron star, previously suggesting a quark star, can instead be explained by significant X-ray flux blocking (factors ≥0.8), yielding canonical neutron star parameters (M~1.59-2.12 M⊙, R~9.8-13.0 km). The variable blocking factor also naturally explains the anomalously high peak-to-touchdown flux ratio.
AI.motivation: To challenge the interpretation that 4U 1746-37 hosts an exotic quark star by showing that the anomalously small mass/radius estimates can be reconciled with canonical neutron star parameters when accounting for significant X-ray flux blocking.
AI.method: Reanalysis of photospheric radius expansion X-ray burst data from 4U 1746-37, incorporating a blocking factor B≥0.8 (reducing observed flux to ~17% of intrinsic emission) to derive revised mass-radius constraints.
AI.result: Under significant blocking, canonical neutron star parameters are recovered: M=1.59±0.69 M⊙, R=13.0±5.45 km, or alternative solution M=2.12±1.08 M⊙, R=9.80±4.13 km. The variable blocking factor also explains the observed peak-to-touchdown flux ratio of ~2.0.
AI.conclusion: Geometric system configuration and flux blocking effects critically impact neutron star mass-radius estimates from X-ray bursts, and need not invoke exotic quark star scenarios for 4U 1746-37.

title: Observation of spontaneous N-bearing PAH formation using ion trap: a new formation pathway in the interstellar medium
summary: Nitrogen-bearing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (N-PAHs) are key precursors to complex organic molecules in both the interstellar medium and the nitrogen-rich planetary atmospheres. Despite the recent detections of nitrogen-functionalized astromolecules, their formation pathways remain an open question. The discrepancies between their predicted and observed abundances point to unknown mechanism that govern their evolution in the astrophysical environments. Employing an ion trap technique and electronic structure calculations, we unravel multiple barrier-less reactions between gas-phase pyrimidine cations (C$_4$H$_4$N$_2^+$) and acetylene (C$_2$H$_2$) which form an hitherto unreported endocyclic- N-PAHs (C$_8$H$_7$N$_2^+$). The present measurements on reactions involving a double-nitrogen subsituted aromatic heterocycle have implications to the astrochemistry of both the Titan's atmosphere and interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This study reveals barrier-less reactions between pyrimidine cations and acetylene forming endocyclic N-PAHs, with implications for astrochemistry in Titan's atmosphere and the interstellar medium.
AI.motivation: N-PAHs are key precursors to complex organic molecules in interstellar and planetary environments, yet their formation pathways remain poorly understood due to discrepancies between predicted and observed abundances.
AI.method: Ion trap technique combined with electronic structure calculations to study gas-phase reactions between pyrimidine cations (C₄H₄N₂⁺) and acetylene (C₂H₂).
AI.result: Multiple barrier-less reactions were identified that form previously unreported endocyclic N-PAHs (C₈H₇N₂⁺).
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a viable formation pathway for endocyclic N-PAHs under astrophysical conditions, with implications for understanding the organic chemistry in Titan's atmosphere and the interstellar medium.

title: Not All Who Wander Are Lost: Early Excess Demographics in the Volume-limited ZTF DR2 SN Ia Sample
comment: Submitted to Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics (RAA). 23 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables (excluding references and appendices); 35 pages total
summary: Early-time flux excesses in Type Ia supernovae (SNe~Ia) offer a unique insight into their progenitor systems and explosion mechanisms. Although individual early-excess events and larger searches have been reported, demographic studies remain limited by sample size. We present a systematic search for early-time excess emission in a volume-limited sample ($z<0.06$) of SNe~Ia based on the Zwicky Transient Facility Data Release 2 (ZTF DR2). Using ZTF $g$- and $r$-band light curves, we identify candidates showing early-excesses shortly after the explosion time, and we apply conservative coverage and quality requirements to build reliable ``excess'' and ``no-excess'' bump and no-bump catalogs. From an initial sample of 1547 SNe~Ia, our final catalogs contain 42 early-excess and 110 no-excess events. We compare the two populations using SN and host environment parameters from ZTF DR2 and quantify the differences using two-sample statistical tests. We find the strongest differences are in SN light-curve properties: early-excess events have larger SALT2 stretch $x_1$ ($7.91σ$) and larger $r$-band secondary-maximum flux $\mathcal{F}_{r_2}$ ($6.25σ$), while differences in SALT2 color $c$ are weak ($0.57σ$). Early-excess events also favor bluer $(g-z)_{\rm local}$ ($3.41σ$) and lower $\log_{10} (M_*/M_\odot)_{\rm local}$ ($2.73σ$). Our results connect early excesses with SNe~Ia diversity, and motivate further analyses of upcoming larger samples.

AI.tldr: A systematic search for early-time flux excesses in 1547 ZTF DR2 SNe Ia (z<0.06) yields 42 excess and 110 no-excess events; early-excess SNe show larger SALT2 stretch x₁, stronger r-band secondary maxima, bluer local (g−z) colors, and lower local stellar mass, linking early excesses to SN Ia diversity.
AI.motivation: Early-time flux excesses in SNe Ia provide unique probes of progenitor systems and explosion mechanisms, but demographic studies are limited by small sample sizes.
AI.method: Systematic search using ZTF DR2 g- and r-band light curves of a volume-limited (z<0.06) sample of 1547 SNe Ia; applied conservative coverage/quality cuts to build excess (42) and no-excess (110) catalogs; compared populations via two-sample statistical tests on SN and host parameters.
AI.result: Early-excess events have significantly larger SALT2 stretch x₁ (7.91σ), stronger r-band secondary-maximum flux (6.25σ), bluer local (g−z) colors (3.41σ), and lower local stellar mass (2.73σ); color c differences are weak (0.57σ).
AI.conclusion: Early excesses are connected to SN Ia diversity, motivating further analyses with larger upcoming samples.

title: GeV emission around SS 433 with 17 years Fermi-LAT observation
summary:
We present an analysis of 17 years of Fermi-LAT observations of the microquasar SS~433. We detect four GeV sources in the region: a newly identified source, PS J1910+0550, located outside W50; the previously reported source J1913+0512; and two features, denoted as the East and West excesses, apparently associated with the X-ray lobes. We focus on the three sources located within W50.
  We do not confirm the previously reported periodic modulation from J1913+0512, as no significant periodicity is found in the full 17-year dataset. The East and West excesses exhibit distinct morphological and spectral properties, suggesting different physical origins. The East excess shows a hard spectrum with photon index $\sim1.7$, consistent with inverse Compton emission from relativistic electrons accelerated together with the particles responsible for the X-ray and TeV emission. In contrast, the West excess has a much softer spectrum with photon index $\sim2.6$ and is spatially offset from the known X-ray and TeV emission regions in the western lobe. The spectral shape and offset position of the West excess make it strikingly similar to J1913+0512.
  The emission from these two regions can be explained by GeV particles accelerated in SS~433, distributed throughout the source volume, and interacting with localized dense gas targets. Under reasonable assumptions regarding particle transport and energetics, both proton-proton and bremsstrahlung scenarios are viable, although the hadronic scenario is more naturally accommodated. These findings may therefore represent the first observational evidence for the acceleration of cosmic-ray protons in large-scale outflows from Galactic microquasars.

AI.tldr: 17-year Fermi-LAT analysis of SS 433 reveals four GeV sources (including a new one, PS J1910+0550), two of which (East and West excesses) have distinct spectra and morphologies. The West excess resembles J1913+0512, and both may arise from GeV particles interacting with dense gas—potentially the first evidence of cosmic-ray proton acceleration in microquasar outflows.
AI.motivation: To investigate the high-energy gamma-ray emission from the microquasar SS 433 using 17 years of Fermi-LAT data, characterize the newly detected sources, and understand the origin of the GeV emission, particularly the potential role of hadronic processes (proton acceleration) in large-scale jets/outflows.
AI.method: Analysis of 17 years of Fermi-LAT data to identify and characterize GeV sources in the SS 433/W50 region, including spectral fitting, morphological analysis, and periodicity searches. Comparisons with X-ray and TeV data were performed to assess multi-wavelength consistency.
AI.result: Detected four GeV sources: a new source PS J1910+0550 (outside W50), previously known J1913+0512, and East/West excesses within W50. No periodic modulation from J1913+0512 was confirmed. The East excess has a hard spectrum (photon index ~1.7) consistent with inverse Compton. The West excess has a soft spectrum (index ~2.6) and is spatially offset from known X-ray/TeV emission, resembling J1913+0512. Both West excess and J1913+0512 can be explained by hadronic (p-p) or bremsstrahlung scenarios, with hadronic being more naturally accommodated.
AI.conclusion: The GeV emission from the West excess and J1913+0512 may represent the first observational evidence for cosmic-ray proton acceleration in large-scale outflows from Galactic microquasars.

title: Discovery of a Compact Hub-Filament System in G286.21+0.17 with JWST and ALMA: Insights into Protocluster Formation and Competitive Accretion
summary: We present a multi-wavelength study of the massive protocluster G286.21+0.17 (G286) using \emph{JWST} near-infrared imaging and ALMA H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$(1--0) observations. The \emph{JWST} images uncover a compact ($\sim$0.5 pc) hub-filament system (HFS), comprising a dense central hub connected by at least four converging filaments seen in absorption, along with multiple H$_2$ protostellar jets/outflows. The hub hosts dense core G286c1. The H$^{13}$CO$^{+}$ emission confirms this HFS over [$-$19.2, $-$16.4]~km~s$^{-1}$. The \emph{JWST} images further trace prominent photodissociation regions around the H\,{\sc ii}~region~A, powered by a B-type star. The radial distribution of ALMAGAL 1.38 mm core properties reveals steep power-law slopes toward the hub center. Within the inner hub (r < 8'', $\sim0.1$~pc), the core number density follows $ρ~[\rm pc^{-2}] \propto r^{-2.4\pm0.5}$, the surface density scales as $Σ~[\rm g~cm^{-2}] \propto r^{-1.0\pm0.2}$, and the enclosed core mass varies as $M_{\rm core}~[M_{\odot}] \propto r^{-1.2\pm0.2}$, while core diameters remain approximately constant ($D_{\rm core}~[\rm AU] \propto r^{-0.1\pm0.1}$). These trends, along with filament mass accretion rates of $7\times10^{-6}$--$1.8\times10^{-4}$~$M_\odot$~yr$^{-1}$, support a competitive accretion scenario in which gravitational focusing enhances core growth toward the hub center. Filament linewidths increase from tail/outer-region to head/hub-region, consistent with gravity-driven turbulence. However, the absence of a preferred alignment between velocity gradients and gravitational force directions may indicate a dynamically evolved system. The HFS likely formed through large-scale gas layer interactions and compression by the adjacent H\,{\sc ii} region. Overall, star formation in G286 appears regulated by filamentary accretion, competitive core growth in the hub, and stellar feedback.

AI.tldr: JWST and ALMA observations of the massive protocluster G286.21+0.17 reveal a compact hub-filament system with converging filaments, protostellar outflows, and photodissociation regions. Core properties show steep radial gradients (density ∝ r⁻²·⁴, surface density ∝ r⁻¹·⁰, enclosed mass ∝ r⁻¹·²) supporting competitive accretion in the hub. Filament accretion rates (7×10⁻⁶–1.8×10⁻⁴ M⊙ yr⁻¹) and gravity-driven turbulence are observed, but misaligned velocity gradients suggest dynamical evolution. The system formed via gas layer interactions and HII region compression.
AI.motivation: To characterize the multi-scale structure and star formation processes in the massive protocluster G286.21+0.17, focusing on how hub-filament systems, core accretion, and stellar feedback regulate high-mass star formation.
AI.method: Combined JWST near-infrared imaging (tracing absorption features, H₂ jets/outflows, and PDRs) with ALMA H¹³CO⁺(1–0) line emission (tracing gas kinematics and filament structure). Radial profiles of ALMAGAL 1.38 mm core properties (number density, surface density, enclosed mass, core diameter) were derived and fit with power laws.
AI.result: (1) Identified a compact (~0.5 pc) hub-filament system with ≥4 converging filaments and a dense central hub (G286c1). (2) Core radial profiles: ρ ∝ r⁻²·⁴±⁰·⁵, Σ ∝ r⁻¹·⁰±⁰·², M_core ∝ r⁻¹·²±⁰·²; core diameter nearly constant (∝ r⁻⁰·¹±⁰·¹). (3) Filament mass accretion rates 7×10⁻⁶–1.8×10⁻⁴ M⊙ yr⁻¹. (4) Filament linewidths increase from tail to hub, but velocity gradients lack alignment with gravitational forces.
AI.conclusion: Star formation in G286 is regulated by filamentary accretion, competitive accretion (gravitational focusing) in the hub, and stellar feedback (HII region compression). The system appears dynamically evolved based on misaligned velocity gradients.

title: Self-confinement of ultra-high-energy nuclei in cosmic filaments: implications for the UHECR spectrum and composition
summary: The spectrum and composition of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) suggest that the population dominating above the ankle releases particles with an unusual hard spectrum at low rigidity, below the EV scale. In self-confinement scenarios, such an apparent hardening arises from transport: escaping UHECRs generate magnetic turbulence that delays their own release from the magnetized environments surrounding their sources. We extend the self-confinement scenario based on the non-resonant streaming instability to a mixed nuclear composition. We describe the confinement region with an effective leaky-box model including escape, photodisintegration, and secondary production. We then compare the resulting spectrum and composition with Auger measurements and compute the associated cosmogenic neutrino and gamma-ray emission. We find that self-generated turbulence can suppress the escaping flux below the EV scale for source luminosities and magnetic-field coherence lengths compatible with UHECR sources hosted in galaxy clusters and propagating through cosmic filaments. During confinement, heavy nuclei efficiently photodisintegrate, producing secondary protons that contribute below the ankle and help account for the observed composition. The predicted neutrino flux remains compatible with current limits, while the diffuse gamma-ray background provides a potentially strong constraint on the most extreme configurations.

AI.tldr: UHECR self-confinement via non-resonant streaming instability with mixed nuclear composition explains the hard spectrum below EV scale, photodisintegration produces secondary protons, and predictions are consistent with Auger data and current neutrino limits while gamma-ray background constrains extreme configurations.
AI.motivation: The unusual hard spectrum of UHECRs below the EV scale cannot be explained solely by source injection; the self-confinement scenario based on non-resonant streaming instability offers a transport-based explanation, but its implications for mixed nuclear composition and multimessenger predictions had not been explored.
AI.method: Extended the self-confinement scenario to mixed nuclear composition using an effective leaky-box model that accounts for escape, photodisintegration, and secondary production; compared resulting spectrum and composition with Auger measurements and computed associated cosmogenic neutrino and gamma-ray emission.
AI.result: Self-generated turbulence suppresses escaping flux below EV scale for source luminosities and magnetic coherence lengths consistent with UHECR sources in galaxy clusters/cosmic filaments; heavy nuclei photodisintegrate during confinement, producing secondary protons that help match observed composition; neutrino flux is compatible with current limits; diffuse gamma-ray background strongly constrains extreme configurations.
AI.conclusion: The self-confinement scenario with mixed composition can explain the spectral hardening and composition of UHECRs, with photodisintegration of heavy nuclei playing a key role, and multimessenger constraints (especially gamma-ray background) providing important discriminators.

title: Boundary-supported radial layering in Hoag-like ring galaxies
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures; submitted to MNRAS Letters
summary: Clean Hoag-like ring galaxies are often characterized by an old compact central component, a depleted gap, and a detached outer ring. We identify a boundary-supported radial-layering mechanism in a shell-deformed Kepler control model. A compact inner boundary supplies the core state, while a localized effective shell deformation, interpreted as the reduced imprint of externally supplied material settled near a finite circularization radius, needs to create only an internal maximum and a subsequent outer minimum. These act as the gap barrier and ring-supporting well. The onset of this structure is organized by a saddle-node threshold of the critical-point equation. In a 10^4-point Monte Carlo scan, shell-localized boundary-supported candidates occupy finite parameter volume under the adopted priors, and none of the localized candidates contains an ordered interior minimum--maximum--minimum subsequence. The same branch gives a scale-free gap-to-ring interval overlapping representative ratios for Hoag's Object, UGC 4599, and PGC 1000714, but not for the environmentally processed comparison object JO171.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a boundary-supported radial-layering mechanism in a shell-deformed Kepler model to explain the formation of clean Hoag-like ring galaxies, where a compact inner boundary provides the core, a localized shell deformation creates a gap barrier and ring-supporting well, and the structure is organized by a saddle-node threshold. Monte Carlo tests show finite parameter volume for such candidates, and the model reproduces gap-to-ring intervals for Hoag's Object, UGC 4599, and PGC 1000714, but not for JO171.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation mechanism of clean Hoag-like ring galaxies, characterized by an old compact core, a depleted gap, and a detached outer ring, which remain poorly explained by existing galaxy formation theories.
AI.method: Development of a shell-deformed Kepler control model with boundary-supported radial layering; identification of a saddle-node threshold organizing the critical-point structure; 10^4-point Monte Carlo scan to test parameter space occupancy.
AI.result: Shell-localized boundary-supported candidates occupy finite parameter volume under adopted priors; none contain an ordered interior minimum-maximum-minimum subsequence; the model yields scale-free gap-to-ring intervals matching observations for Hoag's Object, UGC 4599, and PGC 1000714, but not for the environmentally processed JO171.
AI.conclusion: The proposed radial-layering mechanism successfully reproduces key structural features of clean Hoag-like ring galaxies, distinguishing them from environmentally processed systems like JO171, suggesting a distinct formation pathway.

title: Pulsar scintillation arcs formed from branched flow
summary: Radio waves propagating through the interstellar medium are influenced by variations in plasma density. For spatially localised plasma structures along the line of sight, time-delay Doppler analyses of pulsars often reveal scintillation arcs in the secondary spectrum, frequently exhibiting a parabolic morphology. In the thin-screen approximation, the arc curvature is commonly used to infer the distance to the plasma concentration, which is modelled - via Kirchhoff-Fresnel diffraction theory - as an effective phase screen imposed by the column density of a localised disturbance. Here, we identify several limitations of the thin-screen model that necessitate a fully three-dimensional treatment, without reducing the problem to a projected screen density. We show that the arc curvature can vary depending on the three-dimensional structure of the plasma, rendering it a less reliable indicator of distance. Moreover, when volume propagation is considered, asymmetries and a richer variety of features emerge in the secondary spectrum compared to those predicted by the thin-screen approximation. We conjecture that these phenomena are linked to the onset of branched flow produced by a sequence of weak but correlated scattering events.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies limitations of the thin-screen approximation for modeling scintillation arcs from plasma structures in the interstellar medium, showing that a full three-dimensional treatment reveals distance inference from arc curvature is less reliable, and that volume propagation produces richer spectral features possibly linked to branched flow.
AI.motivation: The thin-screen model is commonly used to infer distances to plasma concentrations via scintillation arc curvature, but its limitations necessitate a more accurate three-dimensional treatment.
AI.method: The authors analyze the thin-screen approximation via Kirchhoff-Fresnel diffraction theory, identify its limitations, and propose a fully three-dimensional propagation model without reducing the problem to a projected screen density.
AI.result: Arc curvature varies with the three-dimensional plasma structure, making it a less reliable distance indicator. Volume propagation produces asymmetries and richer features in the secondary spectrum compared to the thin-screen model. These phenomena are conjectured to relate to branched flow from weak correlated scattering events.
AI.conclusion: The thin-screen approximation is insufficient for accurately modeling scintillation arcs; a three-dimensional treatment is necessary to capture the full phenomenology, and branched flow may explain the observed features.

title: DREAMS. JWST Spectroscopy of a $z=8.3$ Galaxy with an ALMA Dust Continuum Detection: Early Dust, Very High $T_{\rm dust}$, and a Multi-wavelength [OIII] Ratio Discrepancy
summary: We present a deep DREAMS JWST/NIRSpec MSA medium-grating spectrum of MACS0416-Y1, a galaxy at $z=8.312$ with the highest-redshift ALMA dust continuum detection to date, in order to characterize its properties together with archival IFU and ALMA data. The deep NIRSpec spectrum reveals a broad H$β$ line with a width of $\sim1100$ km s$^{-1}$. We interpret it as a broad-line AGN whose line diagnostics are consistent with AGN activity across its clumpy structure, given the absence of little red dot signatures. MACS0416-Y1 clearly shows [OIII]4363 emission, suggesting a moderately low metallicity of $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=7.86^{+0.09}_{-0.08}$ ($0.15~Z_\odot$). The combination of [CII]158$μ$m and dust continuum emission indicates low dust mass ratios of $\log (M_{\rm dust}/M_{\rm gas})=-3.60^{+0.29}_{-0.22}$ and $\log (M_{\rm dust}/M_{\rm metal})=-0.95^{+0.29}_{-0.20}$. Because the metallicity of MACS0416-Y1 is around the critical metallicity of $0.1\textrm{-}0.2~Z_\odot$, the system is expected to undergo dust growth, explaining these low dust mass ratios as well as its small dust mass, $M_{\rm dust}\sim10^6~M_\odot$. The intense UV radiation from the AGN may contribute to a high dust temperature of $T_{\rm dust}\simeq 91^{+62}_{-35}$ K, boosting the dust-continuum emission above the ALMA detection limit despite the small $M_{\rm dust}$ at $z>8$. We find a very high total flux ratio of [OIII]88$μ$m/[OIII]5007 = $0.26 \pm 0.06$ in MACS0416-Y1, above predictions from single ionized nebular models at any electron density. This discrepancy suggests that the [OIII]88$μ$m and [OIII]5007 trace largely distinct regions, with the optical line suppressed in dusty nebulae, and thus requires careful interpretation when combining optical and infrared emission lines in JWST+ALMA studies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents JWST/NIRSpec observations of MACS0416-Y1 (z=8.312), revealing a broad Hβ line (~1100 km/s) indicative of an AGN, low metallicity (0.15 Z☉), very low dust-to-gas and dust-to-metal ratios, high dust temperature (~91 K), and an anomalously high [OIII]88μm/[OIII]5007 flux ratio that suggests these lines trace distinct regions, challenging single-zone nebular models.
AI.motivation: To characterize the physical properties of MACS0416-Y1, the highest-redshift galaxy with ALMA dust continuum detection, using deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy combined with archival IFU and ALMA data, particularly to understand its AGN nature, dust content, metallicity, and the relationship between optical and far-infrared emission lines at high redshift.
AI.method: Deep JWST/NIRSpec MSA medium-grating spectrum of MACS0416-Y1 at z=8.312, complemented by archival IFU and ALMA data. Line width measurements, AGN diagnostics, metallicity determination via [OIII]4363, dust mass and temperature estimation from ALMA continuum and [CII]158μm, and comparison of [OIII]88μm and [OIII]5007 line ratios.
AI.result: (1) Broad Hβ (~1100 km/s) indicating a broad-line AGN without little red dot signatures; (2) low metallicity 12+log(O/H)=7.86 (~0.15 Z☉); (3) very low dust mass ratios: log(M_dust/M_gas)=-3.60, log(M_dust/M_metal)=-0.95; (4) small dust mass ~10^6 M☉; (5) high dust temperature ~91 K; (6) [OIII]88μm/[OIII]5007 flux ratio of 0.26±0.06, exceeding single-zone nebular model predictions.
AI.conclusion: MACS0416-Y1 hosts a broad-line AGN at z>8 with low metallicity near the critical threshold for dust growth, explaining its low dust mass ratios. The AGN's UV radiation may heat dust to high temperatures, enabling ALMA detection despite the small dust mass. The discrepant [OIII] line ratio indicates that optical and far-infrared [OIII] lines trace different nebular regions, requiring careful multi-wavelength interpretation in JWST+ALMA studies.

title: Imaging without visibilities: FAST-Effelsberg scintillometry of PSR B1508+55
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, published in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary:
Context. The spatially coherent multipath propagation of pulsar radiation leads to a temporal and spectral interference patterns called scintillation. It is caused by density variations in the ionized interstellar medium, which often take the form of thin scattering screens filled with multiple subimages of the pulsar. PSR B1508+55 is known to be scattered by one or two such screens.
  Aims. We investigate appropriate methods to achieve precise astrometry for a scattering screen from simultaneous observations of only two telescopes on a very long baseline without forming visibilities. Methods. Two simultaneous observations of PSR B1508+55 were performed with the 100-m telescope at Effelsberg and the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope (FAST). Using and improving existing scintillometry techniques, we leveraged the evolving, very long baseline to precisely measure the screen orientation, effective velocity, and scintillation arc curvature. We inferred the one-screen and two-screen model parameters and we imaged the closer screen.
  Results. Each single epoch leads to much tighter angular constraints than long-term monitoring of scintillation arcs, revealing an ongoing evolution of the orientation of the closer screen. Images of the scattered pulsar were obtained with a resolution on the order of 0.1 mas. These results confirm the highly anisotropic alignment of the scattered images, while also revealing small-scale deviations from a large-scale straight line.
  Conclusions. We demonstrate that simultaneous observations of scintillation can be used as a powerful substitute for very long baseline inferometry.

AI.tldr: Using simultaneous observations from two telescopes (Effelsberg and FAST) without forming visibilities, the authors demonstrate that scintillation techniques can achieve precise astrometry of scattering screens, yielding high-resolution images (~0.1 mas) of PSR B1508+55 and revealing anisotropic, evolving structures in the interstellar medium.
AI.motivation: To investigate methods for precise astrometry of scattering screens using only two telescopes on a very long baseline without forming visibilities, overcoming limitations of traditional long-term monitoring of scintillation arcs.
AI.method: Two simultaneous observations of PSR B1508+55 using the 100-m Effelsberg telescope and FAST. Improved scintillometry techniques leverage the evolving very long baseline to measure screen orientation, effective velocity, and scintillation arc curvature. One-screen and two-screen models were inferred, and the closer screen was imaged.
AI.result: Each single epoch yields much tighter angular constraints than long-term monitoring. Images of the scattered pulsar were obtained with ~0.1 mas resolution, confirming highly anisotropic alignment of scattered images and revealing small-scale deviations from a straight line. The orientation of the closer screen shows ongoing evolution.
AI.conclusion: Simultaneous observations of scintillation can serve as a powerful substitute for very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) for precise astrometry of scattering screens.

title: Identifying group galaxies merging with massive clusters using machine learning
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 18 pages, 17 figures
summary: The environment plays a critical role in galaxy evolution, with galaxy clusters and their infall regions offering diverse conditions that shape galaxies before they enter the dense cluster core, a process known as ``pre-processing''. However, identifying environmental substructures, particularly galaxy groups in these transitional zones, remains challenging due to projection effects and ``fingers-of-god'' distortions. In this work, we present a supervised machine learning framework for classifying galaxies into three environmental categories: main cluster, group, and neither, using observable galaxy properties such as positions, line-of-sight velocities, and stellar mass. The model is trained on mock observations derived from cosmological simulations designed to replicate survey conditions and achieves an overall accuracy and class-size-weighted precision of 81%. The neither and main cluster populations are reliably recovered, whereas group galaxies remain the most challenging to identify, achieving 30% completeness and 76% purity. Within $1\times R_{200}$, classification performance is suppressed, but it improves beyond this radius, reaching 40% completeness and 80% purity. Resampling and thresholding strategies allow the model to be tuned toward either higher purity or higher completeness; in this study, we adopt first-past-the-post thresholding to emphasise purity. Model performance is consistent across cluster masses and dynamical states, and it outperforms both Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Modelling. This flexibility makes it well suited to upcoming spectroscopic surveys of cluster infall regions, providing a robust statistical tool for disentangling environmental influences on galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a supervised machine learning framework to classify galaxies in cluster infall regions into three environmental categories (main cluster, group, neither) using observable properties, achieving 81% accuracy. Group galaxies are hardest to identify (30% completeness, 76% purity). The method outperforms Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Modelling and is robust across cluster masses and dynamical states.
AI.motivation: The environment plays a critical role in galaxy evolution, with galaxy clusters and their infall regions offering diverse conditions that shape galaxies before they enter the dense cluster core (pre-processing). However, identifying environmental substructures, particularly galaxy groups in these transitional zones, remains challenging due to projection effects and fingers-of-god distortions.
AI.method: A supervised machine learning framework that classifies galaxies into three environmental categories (main cluster, group, neither) using observable galaxy properties (positions, line-of-sight velocities, stellar mass). The model is trained on mock observations from cosmological simulations replicating survey conditions. Resampling and thresholding strategies (first-past-the-post thresholding) are used to tune toward higher purity or completeness.
AI.result: Overall accuracy and class-size-weighted precision of 81%. Neither and main cluster populations are reliably recovered; group galaxies achieve 30% completeness and 76% purity. Within 1×R200, classification is suppressed, but beyond this radius it reaches 40% completeness and 80% purity. Model performance is consistent across cluster masses and dynamical states, and outperforms Friends-of-Friends and Gaussian Mixture Modelling.
AI.conclusion: The flexible machine learning framework is well suited to upcoming spectroscopic surveys of cluster infall regions, providing a robust statistical tool for disentangling environmental influences on galaxy evolution.

title: Significant or Not? The Impact of Randomisation During Data Reduction on Confirming a New Pulsating Ultraluminous X-ray Source Candidate in Centaurus A
comment: 23 Pages, 13 Figures. Accepted for Publication in MNRAS. The supplementary material will be hosted on the MNRAS website
summary: We report the discovery of a new candidate pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source (PULX) in NGC 5128 (Centaurus A). The candidate, 4XMM J132542.2-425943, is a transient source, identifiable as a clear X-ray point source for $\sim 8$ months in 2014, during its only major recorded outburst. The source flux exceeded $10^{-12}$ erg cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$ at the peak of the outburst. The long-term light curve of 4XMM J132542.2-425943 shows two further, less luminous detections in 2017 and 2024, but was otherwise in quiescence. This behaviour is similar to the class of pulsating transients with outbursts that reach the ultraluminous regime, which includes the well-studied Galactic PULX, Swift J0243.6+6124. However, 4XMM J132542.2-425943 displays a soft X-ray spectrum, making this source distinct from the existing population of PULXs, which typically show hard spectra below $10$ keV. We searched the 2014 XMM-Newton observations for X-ray pulsations, revealing coherent, sinusoidal X-ray pulsations at a frequency of $1.27$ Hz in one XMM-Newton observation (ObsID 0724060801), at a marginal significance. For this signal we measure a pulsed fraction, PF$\approx~15 - 17~\%$ and $\dot{f}~\sim~4~\times~10^{-9}$ Hz s$^{-1}$. However, we find that the intrinsic randomisation employed by XMM-Newton's Science Analysis Software, XMM-SAS, during the data reduction procedure introduces considerable uncertainty in the strength of our marginal pulsations, which varies significantly between consecutive data reduction iterations. We explore the impact of this randomisation and demonstrate that it can generate widespread false positives and false negatives, which, in the context of PULX searches, may cause viable candidates to be unnecessarily discarded or vice versa.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the discovery of 4XMM J132542.2-425943, a candidate pulsating ultraluminous X-ray source (PULX) in NGC 5128, with a transient outburst in 2014, soft X-ray spectrum, and marginal 1.27 Hz pulsations, while also highlighting how XMM-SAS data reduction randomization can produce false positives/negatives in PULX searches.
AI.motivation: To identify and characterize a new candidate PULX that exhibits a soft X-ray spectrum, distinct from the typically hard-spectrum population, and to investigate the reliability of pulsation detection given artifacts introduced by XMM-SAS randomization.
AI.method: Analysis of long-term X-ray light curves from XMM-Newton for the transient source 4XMM J132542.2-425943; search for coherent X-ray pulsations at ~1.27 Hz; assessment of the impact of XMM-SAS intrinsic randomization on pulsation significance through iterative data reduction.
AI.result: A transient outburst in 2014 reaching >10⁻¹² erg cm⁻² s⁻¹; marginal detection of 1.27 Hz sinusoidal pulsations with pulsed fraction ~15-17% and spin-up rate ~4×10⁻⁹ Hz s⁻¹; soft X-ray spectrum unlike typical PULXs; XMM-SAS randomization introduces large variability in pulsation significance between reduction iterations, causing false positives/negatives.
AI.conclusion: 4XMM J132542.2-425943 is a promising soft-spectrum PULX candidate, but the marginal pulsation signal requires confirmation; the XMM-SAS randomization issue poses a significant challenge for PULX searches, potentially leading to erroneous inclusion or exclusion of candidates.

title: The DESIRED electron temperature relations in star-forming regions of the local Universe
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables (2 longtables online). Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Aims. We present a homogeneous observational study of electron temperature ($T_{\rm e}$) relations between ionic species: $T_{\rm e}$([N II]), $T_{\rm e}$([O II]), $T_{\rm e}$([O III]), $T_{\rm e}$([S II]), $T_{\rm e}$([S III]) and $T_{\rm e}$([Ar III]), using 699 spectra of Galactic and extragalactic H II regions and local star-forming galaxies (SFGs). Methods. We use the DEep Spectra of Ionised REgions Database Extended (DESIRED-E), comprising more than 3000 spectra with direct $T_{\rm e}$ determinations, selecting those with at least two $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics. We recompute electron density ($n_{\rm e}$) and $T_{\rm e}$ using updated atomic data and a consistent methodology. The resulting $T_{\rm e}$--$T_{\rm e}$ relations are analysed using orthogonal distance regression, quantifying total and intrinsic dispersions and comparing slopes with previous works and photoionisation models. Results. Relations involving low-ionisation $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics show large intrinsic dispersions, especially for $T_{\rm e}$([O II]) and $T_{\rm e}$([S II]), likely due to sensitivity to $n_{\rm e}$ inhomogeneities, recombination contributions, and uncertainties. In contrast, relations using $T_{\rm e}$([N II]) show lower dispersions, indicating that this diagnostic provides a more reliable estimate of the low-ionisation zone temperature when only higher-ionisation $T_{\rm e}$ diagnostics are available, despite observational difficulties at low metallicity. Overall, slopes agree with model predictions, particularly for relations with low intrinsic dispersion, such as those involving $T_{\rm e}$([N II]) and $T_{\rm e}$([S III]). These results provide a robust empirical basis for estimating $T_{\rm e}$ when limited diagnostics are available.

AI.tldr: A homogeneous study of electron temperature relations among multiple ionic species in H II regions and star-forming galaxies, using 699 spectra from the DESIRED-E database, finds that Tₑ([N II]) is the most reliable low-ionization temperature diagnostic, while Tₑ([O II]) and Tₑ([S II]) show large intrinsic dispersions due to density inhomogeneities and recombination effects.
AI.motivation: To provide a consistent, homogeneous observational framework for electron temperature relations between different ionic species in H II regions and star-forming galaxies, enabling reliable temperature estimates when only limited diagnostics are available.
AI.method: Analysis of 699 spectra from the DESIRED-E database (3000+ spectra with direct Tₑ determinations) selected for having at least two Tₑ diagnostics. Electron density and temperature were recomputed using updated atomic data and consistent methodology, then Tₑ-Tₑ relations were analyzed via orthogonal distance regression.
AI.result: Low-ionization Tₑ diagnostics show large intrinsic dispersions (especially Tₑ([O II]) and Tₑ([S II])), while Tₑ([N II]) exhibits lower dispersions and is more reliable. Slopes generally agree with photoionization model predictions, particularly for relations with low intrinsic dispersion.
AI.conclusion: Tₑ([N II]) serves as the best proxy for low-ionization zone temperature when only higher-ionization diagnostics are available, and the derived relations provide a robust empirical basis for estimating electron temperatures in the absence of direct measurements.

title: Polarization Signatures from GRMHD Simulations of Black Hole Accretion
comment: Invited chapter for the edited book "X-ray Polarimetry: Detection, Observations, Modeling and the Future" (Eds. Honghui Liu and Adam Ingram), Springer Singapore, expected in 2026
summary: This chapter tells the still-unfolding story of extracting polarization signatures from general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations of accretion disks. In some sense, this effort is premature as there are still very few results of this kind. Much more abundant are phenomenological models. Nevertheless, we feel now is the time to rally the community to this cause. Since the focus of this book is on X-ray polarimetry, we focus exclusively on simulations of accretion onto compact objects. Most of the relevant work so far has been on black hole accretion disks, though neutron stars are also viable targets for X-ray polarimetry. The focus of our chapter is on how X-ray polarimetry coupled with accretion simulations might help us better understand properties of the disks, coronae, and jets that are the dominant components of accreting compact sources. We briefly illustrate the promise of this technique by demonstrating how it has already been used in the case of the Event Horizon Telescope (using radio polarimetry). We also speculate about where this field may be heading in the near future.

AI.tldr: This chapter discusses the emerging field of extracting polarization signatures from general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations of accretion disks, focusing on X-ray polarimetry of compact objects (black holes and neutron stars). It argues for community engagement in this premature effort, demonstrates promise via Event Horizon Telescope radio polarimetry, and speculates on future directions.
AI.motivation: To rally the community toward using X-ray polarimetry coupled with GRMHD accretion simulations to better understand the properties of disks, coronae, and jets in accreting compact sources, as this approach is still in its infancy but holds significant promise.
AI.method: Review and synthesis of existing GRMHD simulations of accretion onto compact objects (black holes and neutron stars) that produce polarization signatures, with a focus on X-ray polarimetry; comparison with phenomenological models; illustration using Event Horizon Telescope radio polarimetry results.
AI.result: The field of extracting polarization signatures from GRMHD simulations is still premature with few results, yet the Event Horizon Telescope's use of radio polarimetry demonstrates the technique's promise for understanding accretion flow properties.
AI.conclusion: X-ray polarimetry combined with GRMHD simulations has strong potential to advance our understanding of accretion disks, coronae, and jets around compact objects, and the community should intensify efforts in this direction despite its current early stage.

title: Probing the IMF in the Early Universe -- Direct measurements in the Boötes I UFD with JWST/NIRCam
summary: The dependence of the stellar initial mass function (IMF) on star-formation environment, particularly at low metallicities and high redshifts, remains poorly constrained. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) are local fossils of high-redshift galaxies hosting old, metal-poor populations, and their resolved stellar populations provide unique pathways to constrain the sub-solar IMF. We investigate the low-mass IMF in the Boötes I (Boo I) UFD with JWST/NIRCam, leveraging its capability to resolve over 10,000 stars reaching $\lesssim0.15 M_{\odot}$, obtaining one of the largest, deepest resolved stellar samples for UFDs. We explore three different functional forms of the IMF with machine learning and statistical techniques, combining forward modeling of synthetic color-magnitude diagrams with simulation-based inference. We find that a single power-law IMF fails to reproduce the observed luminosity function and also deviates from the canonical Salpeter IMF. Our best-fit broken power-law and lognormal IMF parameters are consistent with the Milky Way within 68% confidence level, providing evidence that star formation at metallicities as low as [Fe/H]$\approx-2.4$ follows a similar IMF as in the Milky Way. By treating Boo I as a local relic analogous to a high-redshift galaxy with a stellar mass of $\lesssim10^5 M_{\odot}$ at $z\gtrsim6$, our results provide evidence for the universality of the IMF across both local and high-redshift environments.

AI.tldr: Using JWST/NIRCam to resolve over 10,000 stars down to ~0.15 M☉ in the ultra-faint dwarf galaxy Boötes I, the authors find that the low-mass stellar initial mass function (IMF) at extremely low metallicity ([Fe/H]≈-2.4) is consistent with the Milky Way IMF, supporting IMF universality across environments, including high-redshift analogs.
AI.motivation: The IMF's dependence on environment—especially low metallicity and high redshift—remains poorly constrained. Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) serve as local relics of high-redshift galaxies, offering a unique opportunity to probe the low-mass IMF in extreme, metal-poor conditions.
AI.method: The authors use JWST/NIRCam to resolve >10,000 stars down to ~0.15 M☉ in Boötes I. They test three IMF functional forms (single power-law, broken power-law, lognormal) via machine learning and simulation-based inference, forward-modeling synthetic color-magnitude diagrams to compare with observed luminosity functions.
AI.result: A single power-law IMF fails to reproduce the observed luminosity function and deviates from the Salpeter IMF. Best-fit broken power-law and lognormal IMFs are consistent with the Milky Way IMF within 68% confidence, at metallicities [Fe/H]≈-2.4.
AI.conclusion: The IMF appears universal across environments, from the Milky Way to ultra-faint dwarf galaxies and, by analogy, to high-redshift galaxies (z≳6, stellar mass ≲10⁵ M☉).

title: Impact of stellar population models on the estimated physical properties of galaxies
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, Submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: Accurate estimates of fundamental physical properties of galaxies, such as star formation rates (SFRs) or stellar masses, are essential for testing and constraining models of galaxy formation and evolution. Spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling has become the standard method for deriving these quantities. However, the influence of the underlying stellar population synthesis (SPS) models on the inferred parameters remains poorly quantified. This work investigates how the choice of SPS models affects the estimation of SFRs and stellar masses derived from SED modeling. Four widely used SPS models are applied to a sample of 17 230 galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts, selected from recently published Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope photometric catalogs. SEDs are modeled using the Code for Investigating GALaxy Emission. The analysis is performed in two steps: (i) estimating galaxy properties with each SPS model, and (ii) employing synthetic catalogs to assess the relative impact of model choice on the recovered parameters. Systematic differences are found among the models, with stellar mass estimates varying by up to ~ 0.6 dex and SFRs by up to ~ 0.4 dex between certain model pairs. The choice of stellar population model introduces significant systematic uncertainties in derived galaxy properties. This dependence should be accounted for when interpreting SED-based measurements and comparing results across different studies of galaxy evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different stellar population synthesis (SPS) models affect estimates of star formation rates and stellar masses derived from spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, using 17,230 galaxies from HST and JWST catalogs. Results show systematic differences up to ~0.6 dex for stellar masses and ~0.4 dex for SFRs between models, highlighting significant model-induced uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Accurate estimates of galaxy properties like SFRs and stellar masses are essential for testing galaxy formation and evolution models, but the influence of underlying SPS models on derived parameters remains poorly quantified.
AI.method: Four widely used SPS models were applied to 17,230 galaxies with spectroscopic redshifts from HST and JWST photometric catalogs. SEDs were modeled using Code for Investigating GALaxy Emission (CIGALE). Analysis proceeded in two steps: (i) estimating properties with each SPS model, and (ii) using synthetic catalogs to assess the relative impact of model choice.
AI.result: Systematic differences among models were found: stellar mass estimates vary by up to ~0.6 dex and SFRs by up to ~0.4 dex between certain model pairs.
AI.conclusion: The choice of stellar population model introduces significant systematic uncertainties in derived galaxy properties, which should be accounted for when interpreting SED-based measurements and comparing results across different studies of galaxy evolution.

title: Constraining the Galactic Center Dark Cluster with ELT/MICADO Observations
summary: The Galactic Center hosts the densest known stellar environment in the Milky Way, dominated by the massive black hole Sgr A* and the surrounding nuclear star cluster. Theory predicts that this region should also contain a large population of stellar compact objects (SCOs) - black holes, neutron stars, and white dwarfs - forming a "dark cluster" whose distribution and properties remain observationally unconstrained. These unseen stellar remnants are central to questions of mass segregation, cluster dynamics, and the expected rate of extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) detectable by future gravitational-wave observatories including LISA. Current evidence for SCOs in the Galactic Center is indirect, relying on dynamical mass measurements, X-ray surveys, and a small number of transient sources. Direct detections remain elusive due to crowding, extinction, and the sensitivity limits of existing instruments. We explore how upcoming facilities, in particular the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) with its first-light imager MICADO, can fundamentally transform this field. MICADO's combination of deep photometry, high spatial resolution, and precise astrometry will enable systematic searches for SCO-star binaries via photometric variability and orbital astrometric signatures, as well as direct detection of isolated accreting black holes interacting with the gas-rich Galactic Center environment. We outline the observational pathways, technical challenges, and expected sensitivities, showing that ELT/MICADO observations can provide the first quantitative constraints on the dark cluster population. Establishing these constraints will be pivotal for understanding the dynamical evolution of the Galactic Center, the role of compact remnants in nuclear star clusters, and the astrophysical context of gravitational-wave sources in galactic nuclei.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how the ELT/MICADO instrument can detect stellar compact objects (black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs) in the Galactic Center's "dark cluster" through photometric variability, astrometric signatures, and accretion signatures, providing the first quantitative constraints on this unseen population that is critical for understanding mass segregation, cluster dynamics, and EMRI rates for LISA.
AI.motivation: The Galactic Center's predicted population of stellar compact objects (black holes, neutron stars, white dwarfs) forming a "dark cluster" remains observationally unconstrained, hindering understanding of mass segregation, cluster dynamics, and EMRI rates for future gravitational-wave observatories like LISA.
AI.method: The study outlines observational pathways using ELT's first-light imager MICADO, leveraging its deep photometry, high spatial resolution, and precise astrometry to detect SCO-star binaries via photometric variability and orbital astrometric signatures, and to directly detect isolated accreting black holes interacting with the gas-rich environment.
AI.result: The analysis shows that ELT/MICADO observations can provide the first quantitative constraints on the dark cluster population, overcoming current limitations of crowding, extinction, and sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Establishing constraints on the dark cluster will be pivotal for understanding the dynamical evolution of the Galactic Center, the role of compact remnants in nuclear star clusters, and the astrophysical context of gravitational-wave sources in galactic nuclei.

title: Infrared Line Diagnostics Fail to Constrain Sgr A*'s UV Output
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Sgr A*, the 4 x 10^6 solar-mass supermassive black hole at the Galactic Center, exhibits frequent flaring with X-ray luminosities of L_X ~ 10^35--10^36 erg s^-1, while its ultraviolet (UV) emission remains unconstrained due to extreme extinction (A_V ~ 30 mag). We use JWST/MIRI time-resolved spectroscopy of the central Galactic Center's 0.3 arcsec region to search for mid-infrared emission-line variability driven by Sgr A* flares, comparing the results to CLOUDY photoionization models spanning flare luminosities of L_UV = 10^32--10^39 erg s^-1 in a dense medium. We detect no statistically significant variability in any mid-infrared line, including [Fe II] 5.34 micron, [Ne II] 12.813 micron, [Fe II] 17.936 micron, and [S III] 18.713 micron. Despite expectations of a flare-driven response, we show that the lack of variability is consistent with the physical conditions in the spatially extended line-emitting gas, where light-crossing timescales of ~0.1--10 days and recombination and cooling timescales much longer than the flare timescale suppress any observable response to individual flares. We further find that the predicted emission is continuum dominated and that even the brightest lines are intrinsically weak and broadened by velocities of order 10^3 km s^-1, reducing their contrast against the continuum and limiting their detectability. Extending the analysis to higher-ionization mid-infrared and near-infrared lines does not improve sensitivity. These results demonstrate that infrared emission lines trace a steady-state radiation field rather than individual flaring events, and therefore infrared line diagnostics cannot be used to constrain the instantaneous UV flux of Sgr A*.

AI.tldr: JWST/MIRI observations of Sgr A* show no mid-infrared emission-line variability from flares, consistent with long recombination/cooling timescales and weak line contrast, indicating IR lines trace steady-state radiation rather than individual flaring events.
AI.motivation: To search for mid-infrared emission-line variability driven by Sgr A* flares and determine whether IR line diagnostics can constrain the instantaneous UV flux of Sgr A*, whose UV emission is unconstrained due to extreme extinction (A_V ~ 30 mag).
AI.method: JWST/MIRI time-resolved spectroscopy of the central 0.3 arcsec region around Sgr A*, comparing observed [Fe II] 5.34 µm, [Ne II] 12.813 µm, [Fe II] 17.936 µm, and [S III] 18.713 µm lines to CLOUDY photoionization models over L_UV = 10^32–10^39 erg s^-1 in a dense medium.
AI.result: No statistically significant variability detected in any mid-infrared line. Lack of variability is consistent with light-crossing timescales of ~0.1–10 days and recombination/cooling timescales much longer than flare timescales. Predicted emission is continuum-dominated; even brightest lines are weak and broadened by ~10^3 km/s, reducing contrast.
AI.conclusion: Infrared emission lines trace a steady-state radiation field, not individual flaring events. IR line diagnostics cannot be used to constrain the instantaneous UV flux of Sgr A*.
